entry: System of ideas intended to explain something, developed through reasoning. In everyday use a theory may be any idea about something, and theories can be compared by how well they explain a phenomenon and by the strength of evidence for and against them. In [[Science|science]], a theory is a well-confirmed explanation of nature, framed so that empirical tests could support it or contradict ("falsify") it. Scientific theories are distinguished from [[Hypothesis|hypotheses]], which are individual testable conjectures, and from [[Scientific law|scientific laws]], which describe how nature behaves under certain conditions. Outside science the word is often contrasted with practice, and "in theory" can mean something untested.

Branch of theoretical computer science and mathematics concerned with what problems can be solved on a model of computation, and how efficiently. It asks what the fundamental capabilities and limitations of computers are. The field has three main branches: [[Formal language|formal language]] and automata theory, [[Computability theory|computability theory]], and [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity theory]]. Researchers study abstract models such as the [[Turing machine]], considered the most powerful reasonable model of computation. Any problem that a Turing machine can decide requires only a finite amount of memory. The [[Halting problem|halting problem]] cannot be solved by a Turing machine, a result that underlies much of computability theory. Pioneers include [[Alan Turing]], [[Kurt Gödel]] and [[Claude Shannon]].

Hypothetical coherent framework of physics containing all physical principles. The original concept is the unification of the four fundamental interactions: electromagnetism, the strong and weak nuclear forces, and gravity. The [[Standard Model]] unifies all forces except gravity, and [[General relativity|general relativity]] has not been unified with [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. The two theories conflict at the Planck scale, such as inside a black hole or at the [[Big Bang]]. [[String theory]] is a leading candidate, but it lacks currently testable predictions. Finding such a theory remains one of the major unsolved problems in physics.

Philosophical theory, credited to [[Plato]], that timeless, unchanging Forms are the basis of reality. Forms are absolute, non-physical essences, such as goodness, justice and equality, which physical objects merely imitate or resemble. The theory is a form of realism, asserting that certain ideas are literally real, and of [[Idealism|idealism]], asserting that reality is fundamentally composed of ideas. In Plato's dialogues, [[Socrates]] often claims that only Forms provide genuine knowledge, as opposed to mere opinion. The earlier [[Pythagoras]] may have held a narrower version in which numbers were the essences of things. [[Aristotle]], a student of Plato, rejected the separation of Forms from particulars and argued for forms within substances. The theory is still considered a classical solution to the problem of universals.

Attempted remediation of a [[Health|health]] problem, usually following a [[Medical diagnosis|medical diagnosis]]. Also called medical treatment, therapy has indications and contraindications, and not all therapies are effective. Many can produce unwanted adverse effects. Therapy draws on conventional [[Medicine|medicine]], traditional medicine and alternative medicine. A therapist is a trained professional who offers any modality of therapy. In [[Mental health|mental health]] contexts the term often refers specifically to [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]]. Levels of [[Health care|health care]] classify care by chronology, priority or intensity. Urgent care handles problems that need attention today but are not necessarily emergencies, while emergency care handles medical emergencies. The English word comes from Latin therapīa and Ancient Greek θεραπεία, meaning "curing" or "healing."

2007 American epic period drama film written and directed by [[Paul Thomas Anderson]]. Loosely based on Upton Sinclair's 1927 novel *Oil!*, it stars [[Daniel Day-Lewis]] as Daniel Plainview, a silver miner turned oilman who pursues ruthless wealth during the California oil boom of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The score was composed by [[Radiohead]] guitarist Jonny Greenwood. The film grossed $76.2 million worldwide. It was nominated for eight Academy Awards, winning two: Best Actor for Day-Lewis and Best Cinematography for Robert Elswit.

Type of [[Explosive|explosive]] munition that disperses an aerosol cloud of fuel and ignites it using atmospheric [[Oxygen|oxygen]]. Also called an aerosol bomb or vacuum bomb, it needs no oxidizer of its own, so it is significantly more energetic than conventional explosives of equal weight. Its blast wave lasts significantly longer than that of a conventional explosive, and it is considerably more effective in enclosed spaces such as tunnels, buildings and fortifications. It is unsuitable underwater, at high altitude or in adverse weather. Many types can be fitted to hand-held launchers. The term derives from Greek words for "heat" and "pressure."

Linked sequence of thermodynamic processes that returns a system to its initial state. The working fluid may convert heat from a warm source into useful work and reject the remainder to a cold sink, which makes the cycle a [[Heat|heat]] engine. Run in reverse, the cycle becomes a [[Heat pump|heat pump]] that uses work to move heat from a cold source to a warm sink. Because the system returns to its initial state, its internal energy does not change over the cycle, and the net work equals the net heat transferred. Power cycles include the Rankine cycle of [[Steam turbine|steam turbines]] and the Otto and Diesel cycles of [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engines]]. The net [[Entropy|entropy]] change over a cycle is zero, because entropy is a state function. On a pressure–volume diagram, a clockwise loop indicates a power cycle.

State function whose change is the maximum work a system can perform at constant temperature. Its sign shows whether a process is thermodynamically favorable or forbidden. Because free energy usually contains [[Potential energy|potential energy]], only changes in it are physically meaningful. The [[Gibbs free energy|Gibbs free energy]], G = H − TS, where H is [[Enthalpy|enthalpy]], is most useful for processes at constant pressure and temperature and is the usual choice in chemistry. The Helmholtz free energy, A = U − TS, measures the reversible work obtainable at constant temperature and is the usual choice in physics. [[Hermann von Helmholtz|Hermann von Helmholtz]] introduced the concept in 1882. The Helmholtz function is proportional to the logarithm of the partition function in [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]].

Part of the large-scale [[Ocean|ocean]] circulation driven by global density gradients from surface heat and freshwater [[Flux|fluxes]]. The name combines "thermo-" (temperature) and "haline" (salt content), which together determine seawater density. Wind-driven surface currents such as the [[Gulf Stream]] carry water poleward, where it cools, sinks and eventually flows into the ocean basins. The bulk upwells in the [[Southern Ocean]], while the oldest waters, with a transit time of approximately 1000 years, upwell in the North Pacific. The circulation transports heat and dissolved matter around the globe, strongly affecting [[Climate|climate]]. Its two major limbs are the Atlantic circulation centered in the North Atlantic and the Southern Ocean circulation near [[Antarctica]]. Evidence suggests both are slowing as [[Climate change|climate change]] adds meltwater from ice sheets, and outright collapse of either would increase droughts in its hemisphere while making the other wetter.

Device that measures temperature using a sensor whose change is converted into a numerical value. The sensor may be the bulb of a mercury-in-glass thermometer or an infrared detector, and the change is shown on a scale or digital readout. Thermometers are used in technology, industry, [[Meteorology|meteorology]], medicine and cooking. Early devices included Philo of Byzantium's air-filled tube and the pneumatic fountain of [[Hero of Alexandria]]. In the late 16th and early 17th centuries, [[Galileo Galilei]] and others developed air-filled thermoscopes, which indicated temperature changes without numerical scales. [[Galen]] proposed a fixed reference point of equal parts ice and boiling water. Gabriel Fahrenheit's mercury thermometer, invented in 1714, led to the Fahrenheit scale. The Kelvin scale places [[Absolute zero|absolute zero]] at 0 K.

Second-generation [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapon]] using [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]], also called a hydrogen bomb or H-bomb. X-rays from a fission primary compress a separate fusion stage in the Teller–Ulam configuration, believed to underlie all such weapons. Named for [[Edward Teller]] and Stanisław Ulam, the design was outlined in 1951 with contributions from [[John von Neumann]]. The first full-scale test, Ivy Mike, was carried out by the United States in 1952. The Soviet Union (1955), United Kingdom (1957), China (1966) and France (1968) later developed multi-stage devices. Thermonuclear weapons are the only artificial source of explosions above one megaton of TNT. The [[Tsar Bomba]], the most powerful bomb ever detonated, yielded 50 megatons of TNT. Most current designs derive much of their energy from fast fission of a uranium tamper, which causes high fallout. Their development dominated the [[Nuclear arms race|nuclear arms race]] of the Cold War.

Ability of an [[Organism|organism]] to keep its body temperature within certain boundaries despite very different surrounding temperatures. Endotherms, often called warm-blooded, generate most of their heat through metabolism and keep their temperature relatively constant. Ectotherms, often called cold-blooded, rely mainly on external sources of heat and on behavior to regulate temperature. Thermoconforming organisms simply adopt the surrounding temperature. Hyperthermia occurs when body temperature rises well above normal; humans may experience lethal hyperthermia when the wet bulb temperature is sustained above 35 °C (95 °F) for six hours. [[Hypothermia|Hypothermia]] occurs when core body temperature falls below 35 °C (95 °F). Some animals, such as hibernating [[Bear|bears]] and [[Bat|bats]] in torpor, allow their temperature to drop to conserve energy. Exact data on animal temperature became possible only with the introduction of [[Thermometer|thermometers]].

One of three major [[Clade|clades]] of dinosaurs, alongside [[Ornithischia]] and Sauropodomorpha. Theropods are characterized by hollow bones and three-toed feet with claws. They were ancestrally carnivorous, though some groups evolved to be [[Herbivore|herbivores]] and omnivores. Many coelurosaurs were covered with feathers. Birds evolved from small coelurosaurian theropods in the [[Jurassic]], and around 11,000 living bird species make theropods the only known living group of dinosaurs. Theropods first appeared in the Late [[Triassic]], about 231.4 million years ago, and included most large land carnivores until the end of the [[Cretaceous]], about 66 million years ago. These included [[Tyrannosaurus]] and [[Giganotosaurus]], among the largest land carnivores ever.

Second-largest city in [[Greece]], capital of Central Macedonia (pop., 2021: 319,045). Founded in 315 BC by Cassander of Macedon, who named it after his wife, a half-sister of [[Alexander the Great]], it became the second-largest and wealthiest city of the [[Byzantine Empire]]. Conquered by the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottomans]] in 1430, it was the only Jewish-majority city in Europe from the 16th to the 20th centuries. It passed to the Kingdom of Greece in 1912. Its Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments are a [[World Heritage Site]]. Its main university, Aristotle University, is the largest in Greece and the Balkans.

French football manager, pundit and former player. Henry joined [[Premier League]] club Arsenal in 1999 and became its all-time leading scorer with 228 goals, playing under [[Arsène Wenger]]. He won the Premier League Golden Boot a record four times. He moved to [[La Liga]] club Barcelona in 2007 and was part of its 2008–09 treble, which included the [[UEFA Champions League]]. With France he won the [[FIFA World Cup|1998 FIFA World Cup]], scoring 51 goals in 123 appearances. After retiring in 2014 he became a coach and television pundit, and he managed Monaco.

1958 novel by Nigerian author [[Chinua Achebe]]. Set in colonial Nigeria, it follows Okonkwo, a traditional and influential leader of the fictional Ibo clan of Umuofia who opposes [[Colonialism|colonialism]] and early Christianity. Achebe wrote it while working at the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation, and it was first published by Heinemann in London on June 17, 1958. It is the first of Achebe's "African trilogy," followed by *No Longer at Ease* (1960) and *Arrow of God* (1964). Its title comes from a line in [[W. B. Yeats]]'s 1919 poem "The Second Coming." The novel is a milestone of [[African literature|African literature]], translated into more than fifty languages and listed on [[Time (magazine)|Time's]] "100 Best English-language Novels from 1923 to 2005."

Organosulfur compound of the form R–SH, the sulfur analog of an [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]. The name blends "thio-" with "alcohol," and the prefix comes from Ancient Greek *theion*, "sulfur." Many thiols smell like [[Garlic|garlic]], cabbage or rotten eggs, and they are added as odorants to [[Natural gas|natural gas]], which is naturally odorless. Skunk spray consists mainly of low-molecular-weight thiols, which the human nose can detect at 10 parts per billion. Thiols have lower [[Boiling point|boiling points]] than alcohols because of weaker [[Hydrogen bond|hydrogen bonding]]. They oxidize to disulfides under mild conditions, a reversible process central to [[Redox|redox]] reactions in biology. Thiols are also called mercaptans, a term derived from Latin for "capturing [[Mercury (element)|mercury]]."

Attempted reconquest of the Holy Land, 1189–1192, led by [[Philip II of France]], [[Richard I of England]] and [[Frederick Barbarossa]]. It was launched after [[Saladin]] captured Jerusalem in 1187. The crusaders recaptured Acre and Jaffa and reversed most of Saladin's conquests in the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]], but failed to retake Jerusalem. Frederick Barbarossa died while crossing a river in 1190, before reaching the Holy Land. The 1192 Treaty of Jaffa, between Richard and Saladin, recognized Muslim control of Jerusalem but allowed unarmed Christian pilgrims to visit. The crusader states kept [[Cyprus]] and a narrow coastal strip from Tyre to Jaffa.

British colonies on the Atlantic coast of [[North America]] that formed the original [[United States]]. Founded from 1607, when Jamestown was established in Virginia, they were grouped as the New England, Middle and Southern colonies. Between 1625 and 1775 their population grew from 2,000 to 2.4 million, largely displacing Native Americans. [[Slavery]] was legal in all of them. After the [[French and Indian War]] (1754–1763), tensions with Britain grew over taxation, and colonists invoked the principle of "no taxation without representation." The colonies declared independence in 1776 and fought the [[American Revolutionary War]] with French aid.

Destructive war fought mainly in [[Central Europe]], 1618–1648. An estimated 4.5 to 8 million soldiers and civilians died from battle, [[Famine|famine]] or disease, and parts of Germany reported population declines of more than 50%. Its roots lay in religious conflict within the [[Holy Roman Empire]] after the [[Reformation|Reformation]], and the 1555 Peace of Augsburg was destabilized as Protestantism spread. The war began in 1618 when Protestant Frederick V of the Palatinate replaced Catholic Emperor Ferdinand II as king of Bohemia. Other powers joined, including [[Gustavus Adolphus]] of Sweden, France and the Spanish Habsburgs. The [[Peace of Westphalia]] of 1648 ended the war and granted greater autonomy to states such as Bavaria and Saxony.

Metropolis and [[Capital city|capital]] of the Indian state of [[Kerala]] (pop., 2011: 957,730). Also known as Trivandrum, it lies near the southern tip of the mainland on India's west coast and is a port city. It has India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, and it is among the few cities in the world with both an international airport and an international seaport close to its center. Its metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants. The city is home to the University of Kerala, and India's space program began there, with the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre of the Indian Space Research Organisation. Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple is known as the richest temple in the world. Marthanda Varma made it the capital of the Kingdom of Travancore in the 18th century, and it remained capital of Travancore–Cochin state after independence in 1947 until Kerala was formed in 1956.

Italian Dominican friar, priest, theologian and philosopher. He is the father of [[Thomism|Thomism]], a school of thought that unites theology and philosophy. He synthesized [[Aristotle|Aristotelian]] philosophy with Christian doctrine and argued that God is the source of both natural reason and faith. His Five Ways are arguments for the existence of God. His best-known work, the unfinished [[Summa Theologica|Summa Theologiae]] (1265–1274), is a comprehensive guide to Catholic theology. He also wrote commentaries on Scripture and Aristotle and composed [[Eucharist|Eucharistic]] hymns that remain part of the liturgy. He was canonized as a [[Saint|saint]] in 1323, and as one of the 38 Doctors of the Church he is known as the Angelic Doctor. His ideas influenced later [[Western philosophy|Western philosophy]] and modern virtue ethics.

English theologian and leader of the [[Reformation|English Reformation]], Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533 to 1555. He helped build the case for annulling [[Henry VIII|Henry VIII]]'s marriage to [[Catherine of Aragon]], which contributed to England's separation from the [[Holy See]]. He supported royal supremacy alongside [[Thomas Cromwell]]. Under Edward VI he compiled the first two editions of the Book of Common Prayer and changed doctrine on the Eucharist, clerical celibacy and the veneration of saints. After the accession of the Catholic [[Mary I]] in 1553 he was tried for treason and [[Heresy|heresy]]. He recanted several times, but on the day of his execution he publicly withdrew his recantations and was burned at the stake. He is honored as a martyr in the [[Church of England]].

English statesman and lawyer, chief minister to Henry VIII from 1534 until mid-1540. As the king's chief secretary, he reorganized government and helped engineer the annulment of the king's marriage to [[Catherine of Aragon]], after which Parliament named Henry Supreme Head of the [[Church of England]]. He played a prominent role in the downfall and 1536 execution of Anne Boleyn. He was created Earl of Essex in 1540 but fell from power after arranging Henry's marriage to Anne of Cleves, which was annulled six months later. He was executed for treason and [[Heresy|heresy]] on Tower Hill.
